clue.text: At which a pound of flesh is a bargain ?

definitions.text: At which a pound of flesh is a bargain ?

parts.words: At which a pound of flesh is a bargain ?
parts.note: Shylock's bond demands a pound of flesh to be cut; read the price as a cut, and a reduced charge is a bargain

explanation.surface: A grim haggle over Shylock's bond from The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: The pound of flesh in The Merchant of Venice was to be cut from the debtor, so a price paid in a cut is a bargain rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A reduced, discounted price is what shoppers call a bargain.

clue.text: One takes no end of cash in, finishing with nothing

indicators.note: the word loses its end letter

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A gambler takes in cash until finishing with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end of' drops the last letter of CASH, giving CAS. A gaming house takes the punters' money, hence 'One takes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambling house rakes in bets, so it is an establishment that takes money.

clue.text: Hockey player, making a hundred to nothing

annotationWithheld.why: Hockey player, making a hundred to nothing (6): scan confirms the text; 'Hockey player' can be a truant playing hookey, but no parse of 'making a hundred to nothing' gives TRUANT
annotationWithheld.clue: Hockey player, making a hundred to nothing

clue.text: Kind of course at the bar ?

definitions.text: Kind of course at the bar ?

parts.words: Kind of course at the bar ?
parts.note: a short course updating skills; also a drink at a bar, and the extra fee paid to a barrister in a long case

explanation.surface: A drinker wonders what sort of course is being served at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the bar' is both a pub counter and the legal profession; a barrister's daily fee for a lengthy case, a drink, and a short training course all share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A brush-up course renews skills, as a drink or a barrister's extra fee renews energy or payment.

clue.text: "'Tis all a — of Nights and Days (Fitzgerald)

definitions.text: "'Tis all a — of Nights and Days (Fitzgerald)

parts.words: "'Tis all a — of Nights and Days (Fitzgerald)
parts.note: a line from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, comparing life to a game board of dark and light squares

explanation.surface: A quotation from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rubaiyat continues 'Where Destiny with Men for Pieces plays': nights and days are the dark and light squares.
explanation.definitionFit: A game board of alternating dark and light squares matches nights alternating with days.

clue.text: Small bird is plucked

parts.note: reads like poultry being prepared, but 'plucked' is the old sense of having pluck, describing a small, famously spirited fowl

explanation.surface: A little bird has had its feathers pulled out ready for the pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucked' looks like the cook's job, but it means full of pluck: this small breed of chicken is known for its aggression, which is why boxing names a light weight after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A miniature breed of domestic fowl, noted for its fighting spirit.

clue.text: Wolf emerges from a turbulent lake

indicators.note: turbulent water is churned up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A wolf rises out of a choppy lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges LAKE into KELA after A. In Kipling's Jungle Book the wolf pack's leader bears this name, used also for a Cub Scout leader.
explanation.definitionFit: The head wolf of the pack in Kipling's Jungle Book.

clue.text: What they call in America " the end "?

parts.note: a term is a name for something, what they call it
taken as written
US is the United States, America

explanation.surface: Asking what Americans call the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue poses as a question about American usage; 'America' is only the abbreviation of the United States, and 'the end' in quotation marks is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The final stop of a railway or bus line is the end of the route.

clue.text: Pickle with butter coming up in cooked tea ?

indicators.note: in a down entry the word rises, so it is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a ram butts with its head, so is a butter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe for steeping food with butter and tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns RAM into MAR; 'cooked' rearranges TEA into ATE. 'butter' is not the dairy spread but one who butts.
explanation.definitionFit: To steep food in a seasoned liquid, much as one pickles it.

clue.text: Behaved shiftily before embarking on the deal

definitions.meaning: to act evasively, moving about and dodging
what is done to a pack of cards before the dealer hands them out

explanation.surface: A dodgy negotiator fidgets evasively before closing a business deal.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both dodging evasively and mixing a pack of cards before dealing.

clue.text: Cheque-cashing porter ?

definitions.meaning: a cheque payable to whoever presents it is made out to this person

explanation.surface: A hotel porter is sent to the bank to cash a cheque.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the presenter of an open cheque and a carrier of loads are called by this word.

clue.text: There's the rub — one accurate if misguided description of officialdom

indicators.note: the words, if led astray, are mixed up, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A remark about how accurate a description of red tape is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if misguided' rearranges RUB, I (one) and ACCURATE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape and rule-bound administration are what this adjective describes.

clue.text: There's not anyone round about for the time being

indicators.note: the word for 'not anyone' goes round the abbreviation, enclosing it

parts.note: not anyone means none
C (circa) is the abbreviation for about

explanation.surface: An empty room: nobody is around at present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts NONE about C, the abbreviation of circa. 'For the nonce' is an old phrase meaning for the present occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Used in 'for the nonce', meaning the present occasion or moment.

clue.text: Woeful sound shows Lulu's back getting into a lot of trouble

indicators.note: the singer's name is read from its end, backwards

parts.note: taken as written, the singer's name

indicators.note: the following words are in a troubled state, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Pop singer Lulu, returning to the stage, finds herself in a heap of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LULU into ULUL; 'lot of trouble' rearranges INTO A into ATION. 'into a lot of trouble' reads as one phrase, but 'into a' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A howl or wail of grief is a woeful cry.

clue.text: Old Pretender's sister as impersonated on stage ?

definitions.text: Old Pretender's sister as impersonated on stage ?

parts.words: Old Pretender's sister as impersonated on stage ?
parts.note: the Old Pretender's son was Charles, Bonnie Prince Charlie, so his father's sister is Charlie's aunt; also a farce where a man impersonates an aunt

explanation.surface: A Jacobite princess is portrayed in a stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Pretender, James Stuart, was father of Bonnie Prince Charlie, so his sister is that prince's aunt; Brandon Thomas's 1892 farce has an undergraduate posing as a rich aunt from Brazil.
explanation.definitionFit: A Victorian farce in which an Oxford student dresses up as a wealthy aunt.

clue.text: Direction to player to substitute one letter for two others

definitions.text: Direction to player to substitute one letter for two others

parts.words: Direction to player to substitute one letter for two others
parts.note: a musical instruction; read as an English phrase it says one letter, S, for two others, Z and O

explanation.surface: A musician is told to swap one letter for two.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical term for a sudden strong accent, split as S FOR Z AND O, describes putting S in place of Z and O.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian marking telling a performer to play a note with sudden force.

clue.text: Glasses for those used to having a nip

definitions.text: Glasses for those used to having a nip

parts.words: Glasses for those used to having a nip
parts.note: glasses suggest drinks and a nip a dram, but these spectacles clip onto the nose, their French name meaning 'pinch-nose'

explanation.surface: Drinking glasses for people fond of a tot of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glasses' and 'nip' suggest drinking, but these spectacles grip the bridge of the nose with a spring.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles held in place by a spring clip pinching the nose.

clue.text: Direct view about revolutionary art

indicators.note: the word for view goes round the other piece

parts.note: a sight is a view

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the word is reversed

explanation.surface: A frank opinion on revolutionary art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns the art backwards, giving TRA, and 'about' wraps the view around it; 'view' suggests an opinion but means a sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Going without detours or evasion, as in a frank, direct answer.

clue.text: Oil current to be dispersed by Christy's slick performer

indicators.note: the words before are to be scattered, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An oil spill is broken up by a man named Christy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be dispersed' rearranges OIL CURRENT TO; 'slick' suggests an oil slick but means smooth-talking. The Christy Minstrels were a blackface minstrel troupe whose master of ceremonies traded patter with the end-men.
explanation.definitionFit: In a minstrel show the middleman who leads the banter with the end-men holds this title.

clue.text: Get on a bit, anyway

indicators.note: in any way at all, so the letters may go in any order

explanation.surface: Get on with it, at least a little, anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges ON A BIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquire or gain something is to get it.

clue.text: The poet's always under the car of course

indicators.note: in a down entry the poetic word sits below the other piece

parts.note: taken as written
poets contract ever to e'er

explanation.surface: A poet forever lying beneath a car, of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' seems a filler phrase, but 'course' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapid run or path, as in the course or career of a horse.

clue.text: A bird with a lot of small talk

definitions.meaning: a name for several noisy birds, such as the waxwing

definitions.text: with a lot of small talk

explanation.surface: A talkative bird keeps up a constant stream of gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a garrulous person and certain noisy birds go by this name.

clue.text: Leigh Hunt hoped Abou Ben Adhem's might increase

definitions.text: Leigh Hunt hoped Abou Ben Adhem's might increase

parts.words: Leigh Hunt hoped Abou Ben Adhem's might increase
parts.note: the poem 'Abou Ben Adhem' by Leigh Hunt opens 'Abou Ben Adhem (may his ... increase!)'

explanation.surface: The poet's wish that his hero's kin might multiply.
explanation.walkthrough: Leigh Hunt's poem begins 'Abou Ben Adhem (may his tribe increase!)'.
explanation.definitionFit: A people or clan, the kin of a person, which the poet wished to grow.

clue.text: He helps one across, the beast!

definitions.meaning: a striped pedestrian crossing that helps people cross the road

explanation.surface: A crossword helper is cursed as a brute.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a ZEBRA crossing is a road crossing marked with black and white stripes.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped road crossing and the striped wild horse share the name.

clue.text: Going North perhaps for a drink

indicators.note: the word could perhaps be rearranged, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: Heading north in search of a drink at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: N for North starts the answer, then 'perhaps' rearranges GOING into OGGIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A small measure of liquor, about a quarter of a pint.

clue.text: Time was when all Jaques' world held one

indicators.note: the world of Jaques encloses the other word, holding it inside

parts.note: Jaques in As You Like It says all the world's a stage
taken as written

explanation.surface: Recalling an age when Shakespeare's melancholy Jaques held the whole world in view.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's speech in As You Like It begins 'All the world's a stage'. 'Time was when' defines an era long past, read as a noun phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The prehistoric period when tools were made of flint is a remote era of the past.

clue.text: Music-maker's last letter takes it to her

parts.note: Z is the last letter of the alphabet
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A musician's final letter is passed on to his lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last letter' suggests the end of a written letter, but means Z, the end of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A stringed instrument plucked flat on a table produces music.

clue.text: Hesperus more readily embraces a man of honour

indicators.note: the word for 'more readily' holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: sooner means more readily, as in I'd sooner stay
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: An evening star more willingly takes a gentleman in her arms.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's poem 'The Wreck of the Hesperus' opens 'It was the schooner Hesperus'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ship in Longfellow's poem is an example of a two-masted sailing vessel.
